items.title: Quantitative easing is not 'printing money'
items.claim: Central banks engaged in QE after 2008 and again in 2020-21. Which describes the operation most accurately?

options.text: Central banks printed physical banknotes and gave them to households
Central banks created reserves electronically and used them to buy government bonds (and other assets) from financial institutions; reserves are central bank liabilities, not currency in circulation
QE doubled the M2 money supply directly

items.reveal:
By 2022, the Bank of England's gilt holdings under QE reached £895bn; the Fed's balance sheet peaked near $9 trillion. The reserves created are held by banks at the central bank; they don't enter the real economy as cash.

The mechanism is meant to lower long-term interest rates, support asset prices and ease financial conditions. Whether QE caused 2021-22 inflation is debated; the consensus is the energy shock and pandemic supply disruptions were the dominant drivers, with QE perhaps contributing at the margin.
items.why: 'Printing money' is a misleading shorthand for QE that conflates electronic reserve creation with currency issuance. The mechanisms have different implications.

items.title: Perfect competition is a benchmark, not a description
items.claim: Perfect competition (many small firms, homogeneous products, free entry, perfect information) is taught as a foundational market structure. Which is most accurate?

options.text: Most real markets fit the model closely
Real-world markets rarely satisfy the assumptions; agriculture, currency trading and some commodity markets come closer than most. The model is useful as a normative benchmark, not as descriptive
Perfect competition is identical to monopoly
No real-world market resembles it at all

items.reveal:
Monopolistic competition (Chamberlin 1933) and game-theoretic oligopoly models (Cournot 1838, Bertrand 1883, Stackelberg 1934) capture more of the realistic market structures.

Key deviations: most product markets have differentiated products; information is imperfect (Akerlof's 'lemons' 1970); entry has costs; small numbers of dominant firms common. The 'IO revolution' from the 1970s onwards (Tirole's textbook, 1988) built strategic-interaction-based frameworks.
items.why: The perfect competition model serves as a welfare benchmark in policy analysis. Treating it as a description of how markets work misses what most of industrial economics has been building toward.

items.title: Potential GDP is not directly observable
items.claim: The output gap is actual GDP minus potential GDP, expressed as a percentage of potential. Why is this concept difficult to use in practice?

options.text: Potential GDP is unobservable — it must be estimated, and estimates are revised heavily after the fact. Pre-2008 estimates of potential GDP have been revised down substantially, suggesting the economy was less overheated than thought
It is observable directly from satellite

items.reveal_title: A concept whose measurement is treacherous
items.reveal:
OECD, IMF and central bank estimates of potential GDP use filters (Hodrick-Prescott, Kalman) and production function approaches. They produce different numbers and revise heavily as data arrives.

Orphanides's 2003 paper showed that real-time output gap estimates available to the Fed in the 1970s were systematically wrong, contributing to policy errors.

The BIS has criticised reliance on output gaps for monetary policy.
items.why: Policy variables that depend on unobservable concepts inherit estimation uncertainty. Output gap-based 'rules' look cleaner in textbooks than in practice.
